explanation: Breadth-first search visits reachable white cells once and records each predecessor. On reaching the destination, follow predecessors back to the start and reverse the path. The input maze is unchanged.
timeComplexity: O(r · c). Every reached cell has at most four neighbors and is recorded or marked once; the worst-case frontier/path visits the whole maze.
spaceComplexity: O(r · c), including visited cells, predecessors and queue. Predecessors/frontier or visited markings/path can involve every maze cell; C++ also stores a maze copy.
attribution: Original C# implementation and explanation authored for EPI Practice from the displayed problem contract.
correctness: Every queued cell is an in-bounds white cell reachable from start through its recorded predecessor chain. Adding a previously unseen orthogonal white neighbor preserves this property and ensures each cell is queued once. Reaching end reconstructs a valid endpoint-inclusive path. If the queue empties, every reachable white cell has been explored, so no path exists.
walkthrough: For maze [[0,0,1],[1,0,0],[0,0,0]], start (0,0) and end (2,2), BFS can discover (0,0)→(0,1)→(1,1)→(2,1)→(2,2). Every step is orthogonal and every visited cell is white, so return that path; the judge validates it as true. JSON arguments are [maze,[startRow,startColumn],[endRow,endColumn]]. Observed true means a valid path was accepted; observed false for distinct unreachable endpoints corresponds to an empty returned path. The wrapper also observes true for any empty result when start=end, a weaker check than the callable’s path contract.
edgeCases: Blocked endpoints cannot be used in a path.
A white start equal to end returns a one-cell path.
Unreachable destinations return an empty list.
The original maze is not modified to mark visits.
